name: Amazon CloudWatch
summary: AWS’s built-in monitoring service: metrics from every AWS service, logs, alarms and dashboards, and now traces, OpenTelemetry and PromQL, billed per metric, per GB and per alarm.
intro: Most AWS services publish metrics to CloudWatch automatically and at no charge; EC2, for example, reports every five minutes, or every minute if you pay for detailed monitoring. You add your own numbers with the `PutMetricData` API or, since June 2026, as OpenTelemetry metrics sent over OTLP, which CloudWatch keeps for 15 months and lets you query in PromQL. A classic metric is identified by a namespace, a name and up to 30 dimensions; CloudWatch keeps 1-minute points for 15 days, 5-minute points for 63 days and hourly points for 455 days. Alarms compare a metric with a threshold and, when it’s crossed, notify an SNS topic, scale an Auto Scaling group, stop or recover an EC2 instance, or invoke a Lambda function. Dashboards chart metrics and logs, across accounts and Regions if you want.

CloudWatch Logs stores log events in log groups and streams. Lambda sends every function’s logs there by default, and the CloudWatch agent ships files from EC2 and on-premises servers. Logs Insights queries them in its own query language, OpenSearch PPL or SQL, billed per GB scanned; metric filters turn matching lines into metrics you can alarm on, and subscription filters stream events to Kinesis, Firehose, Lambda or OpenSearch. Log data is kept forever unless you set a retention period on the group.

Around that core AWS keeps adding services under the CloudWatch name: Synthetics canaries (scheduled scripts in Node.js, Python or Java that run as Lambda functions against your endpoints), RUM for real browser sessions, Application Signals for automatic latency, error and request dashboards with SLOs, Container, Lambda and Database Insights, and tracing: X-Ray’s trace map and traces now live in the CloudWatch console, and Transaction Search can store every span as structured logs. In September 2026 AWS launched CloudWatch Omni, an AI-assisted layer that discovers services from your telemetry and writes SQL or PromQL from plain-language questions. The X-Ray SDKs and daemon entered maintenance mode in February 2026, and AWS recommends OpenTelemetry instead.
strengths: Already on: AWS services send metrics, and often logs, with no setup, and basic metrics cost nothing
Alarms act on AWS directly: scale an Auto Scaling group, recover an instance, page through SNS, run a Lambda function
Native OTLP endpoints for metrics, logs and traces, and PromQL for metrics, so instrumentation and queries aren’t CloudWatch-specific
Cross-account observability: one monitoring account can see metrics, logs and traces from many source accounts, linked through AWS Organizations
limits: Many meters: custom metrics, GB of logs ingested and stored, GB scanned by queries, alarms, canary runs, RUM events and each Insights feature. A dimension with many values multiplies classic custom metrics, each billed per month
Log groups keep data forever by default, so storage grows until someone sets a retention period
Two metric systems side by side, Classic (per metric, Metrics Insights) and OpenTelemetry (per GB, PromQL), with different prices and query languages
Built around AWS accounts and Regions: other clouds and on-premises servers need the CloudWatch agent or an OpenTelemetry collector to send data in

sections.title: What you pay for
sections.intro: The main meters, as the CloudWatch pricing page’s worked examples use them for US East. Other Regions differ, and most features have a small free tier.

rows.label: Basic metrics from AWS services
values: EC2 at 5-minute resolution; 1-minute detailed monitoring is charged per metric

rows.label: Custom metrics (Classic)
values: $0.30 per metric per month for the first 10,000
$0.10 from 10,001 to 250,000, less beyond; each unique combination of dimensions is a separate metric

rows.label: OpenTelemetry metrics
values: Includes 15 months of storage, with no charge per series or per API call

rows.label: Logs ingested (Standard class)
values: Storage is billed per GB compressed; the Infrequent Access class has a lower ingestion price and a subset of features

rows.label: Logs Insights queries
values: Narrow the time range and log groups to scan less

rows.label: Alarms
values: $0.10 per standard-resolution alarm metric per month
$0.30 for high resolution; $0.50 per composite alarm

rows.label: Live Tail
values: Streaming log events to the console as they arrive

story: CloudWatch launched in public beta on 18 May 2009, together with Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling, as three parts of one idea: measure EC2 instances and load balancers (CPU, disk and network use, request rates and latency) and act on the numbers automatically. Werner Vogels wrote that Amazon itself monitored every resource in real time and automated new capacity from that data, and the launch gave customers the same tools. Auto Scaling ran on CloudWatch metrics from the first day, at no extra charge.

The service grew outward from EC2: custom metrics for your own numbers in May 2011, CloudWatch Logs for operating system and application log files in July 2014, dashboards in October 2015, Logs Insights for interactive log queries in November 2018, Synthetics canaries generally available in April 2020, real-user monitoring in November 2021, and Application Signals for application performance monitoring in June 2024.

In 2026 AWS moved CloudWatch onto open standards: native OpenTelemetry metrics with PromQL in June, managed Prometheus collectors in July and, in September, CloudWatch Omni, which also brings in Azure workloads. X-Ray’s traces moved into the CloudWatch console, and its own SDKs gave way to OpenTelemetry.

choices.choice: Free basic metrics for every AWS service
choices.why: Monitoring came bundled so that customers could build scaling and recovery on it without deploying anything. Auto Scaling ran on that data from the first day.

choices.choice: Older data rolled up, not deleted
choices.why: CloudWatch keeps full 1-minute resolution for 15 days, then 5-minute points to 63 days and hourly points to 455 days, so you get 15 months of history without keeping every raw point.

choices.choice: Logs as a separate store, joined by metric filters
choices.why: CloudWatch Logs arrived five years after metrics. Metric filters extract numbers from log lines and turn them into CloudWatch metrics, so the same alarms and Auto Scaling actions work on log data.

AWS’s own pitch for the 2026 change: teams already using OpenTelemetry, Prometheus or Grafana can make CloudWatch a destination that fits their existing tools, instead of rewriting instrumentation and queries.
